name: Supply chain / inventory real-time stock & velocity
category: New — supply-chain real-time stock and velocity features
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: Supply chain and inventory real-time stock and velocity features for operations / fulfillment — per-SKU / per-DC sell-through rate, per-(SKU, zone) reservation velocity, per-store stock-out velocity, per-supplier inbound-delay velocity, per-(SKU, channel) attach-rate, per-(SKU, location) days-of-cover, available-to-promise (ATP) inventory counters, ship-from-store / BOPIS routing eligibility features, distributed-order-management (DOM) sourcing-cost / reservation-pressure signals, transportation-visibility ETA-deviation and dwell-time features. The buyer surface is operations / fulfillment / supply-chain-engineering (Manhattan Active OMS / WMS, Blue Yonder OMS+WMS, Oracle Fusion SCM, IBM Sterling, SAP EWM, Fluent Commerce, Kibo, KBRW, OneStock, Aptean Logility, Infios) and the real-time transportation visibility / 3PL control-tower stack (project44, FourKites, Shippeo, Transporeon, Descartes, Vizion, Tive, Tive, Roambee), distinct from the pricing / revenue-management buyer covered in item 12.
domain_fit.one_line_definition: A fulfillment / replenishment / order-orchestration system (omnichannel OMS, WMS, distributed-order-management router, control-tower, 3PL visibility platform, vending / managed-inventory engine) decides — within tens to a few hundred milliseconds on the hot ATP / sourcing / promise-date path, and within seconds-to-minutes on the auto-replenish / auto-reorder path — where to source, when to reorder, when to mark out-of-stock, and how to route an order, on the basis of per-SKU / per-DC / per-store / per-zone rolling sell-through, reservation, stock-out, supplier-delay, and attach-rate counters.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: 1) Maintain per-(SKU, DC) sell-through rate over rolling 1h / 24h / 7d / 30d / 90d windows = count(unit_sold, W) / received_qty_W so a replenishment planner (or a Walmart-style real-time replenishment system) can decide intra-day transfers and reorders. Walmart's published replenishment system processes ~4B messages / <3h across ~100M SKUs at ~85 GB/min through Kafka — exactly the load shape beava counters address. 2) Maintain per-(SKU, store) and per-(SKU, zone) reservation velocity (count of soft reservations, cart-holds, BOPIS-pickup-holds opened vs released in a rolling 5m / 15m / 1h window) so a distributed-order-management router can balance against fresh stock without overselling. 3) Maintain per-store stock-out velocity — count(unit_sold, 5m) divided by remaining on_hand, plus 'time-to-stock-out at current velocity' projections, plus count(stock_out_event, 24h) per (SKU, store) — to drive auto-markdown / auto-substitution / auto-substitute-and-promise-anyway logic (the Instacart 'item availability' problem). 4) Maintain per-supplier and per-(supplier, item_class) inbound-delay velocity — count(late_arrival, 30d), velocity(promised_vs_actual_lead_time, 7d/30d/90d), distribution(actual_lead_time, 90d) for an ML lead-time predictor (the GAINSystems / SAP / Amazon SCM 'dynamic lead-time' pattern). 5) Maintain per-(SKU, channel) attach-rate features (count(co_purchase, W) / count(anchor_purchase, W) per (anchor_sku, candidate_sku, channel)) so the fulfillment / promotions engine can stage co-shipped accessories at the right node. 6) Maintain per-(carrier, lane) and per-(shipment_id) ETA-deviation and dwell-time velocity for project44 / FourKites-style transportation visibility — count(geofence_dwell, 1h), velocity(eta_revision, lane, 24h), distance(predicted_eta - promised_eta). 7) Compute live available-to-promise (ATP) counters: on_hand − soft_reserved − allocated + inbound_in_transit per (SKU, node), refreshed on every order / reservation / receipt event. 8) Drive auto-reorder, auto-rebalance, and auto-substitute triggers from threshold crossings ('when (sku, store).days_of_cover < 3 then call /reorder', 'when (sku, store).stock_out_velocity > N then mark unavailable for online sale and propose substitute').
domain_fit.event_shapes: @bv.event types landing in beava on the hot path: sale {ts, sku, store_id, dc_id, qty, channel, order_id} — the per-unit-sold event that drives sell-through; receipt {ts, sku, dc_id, store_id, qty, po_id, supplier_id, asn_id} — inbound goods arrival; reservation_open {ts, sku, node_id, qty, order_id, hold_type (cart|bopis|pickup|allocated)} and reservation_release {ts, ...} — the soft-reservation lifecycle; cart_add / cart_abandon for ATP soft-hold; allocation {ts, order_id, sku, qty, node_id} — DOM allocation decision; stock_count {ts, sku, node_id, on_hand_qty, source (rfid|cycle_count|pos_correction|ecom_correction)}; transfer_init / transfer_complete {ts, sku, from_node, to_node, qty}; supplier_po_event {ts, po_id, supplier_id, line_items[], promised_dock_date, actual_dock_date}; asn_received {ts, asn_id, supplier_id, sku, qty, expected_dock_date}; carrier_pickup, geofence_dwell {ts, shipment_id, carrier_id, lane_id, h3, dwell_seconds}, eta_revision {ts, shipment_id, lane_id, prev_eta, new_eta, delta_sec}, pod {ts, shipment_id, dock_id}; rfid_read {ts, epc, store_id, zone_id} (Target / Walmart RFID); vending_dispense {ts, fmi_device_id, sku, qty, customer_id} (Fastenal FMI, Grainger KeepStock); stock_out_event {ts, sku, store_id, detected_via (rfid|shopper_observation|cart_failure)}; rebalance_decision {ts, sku, from_node, to_node, qty, reason}. Composite keys are (sku, store_id), (sku, dc_id), (sku, zone_id), (sku, channel), (sku, h3_cell), (supplier_id, sku), (carrier_id, lane_id), (shipment_id), (po_id), (asn_id). Walmart and Instacart published volumes show ~500M events/day inventory-only at Walmart and tens of millions of item-availability scoring events/day at Instacart across 100M+ items.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Heavy use of beava counters + velocity + distance + distribution primitives over sliding and tumbling windows. Per-(SKU, DC): sell_through_W = count(sale, W) / received_qty_W for W in {1h, 24h, 7d, 30d, 90d}; velocity(sale, 24h); days_of_cover = on_hand_now / velocity(sale, 7d); velocity(receipt, 7d); count(stock_out, 24h); on_hand_now (running counter); allocated_now; available_to_promise = on_hand − allocated − soft_reserved + inbound_in_transit. Per-(SKU, store): same as above plus stock_out_velocity = count(sale, 5m) / max(on_hand, ε); time_to_stockout_seconds = on_hand / velocity(sale, 1h); count(rfid_correction, 24h) as accuracy signal. Per-(SKU, zone): reservation_open_count(15m), reservation_release_count(15m), net_reservation_pressure = open − release. Per-(SKU, channel): attach_rate = count(line_with_anchor_AND_candidate, 7d) / count(line_with_anchor, 7d) per (anchor_sku, candidate_sku, channel). Per-supplier: late_arrival_count(30d), velocity(promised_vs_actual_lead_time_delta, 90d), distribution(actual_lead_time, 90d) (T-Digest for p50 / p90 / p99 supplier lead-time), on_time_rate_30d = on_time / total, count(fill_rate_breach, 30d), distance(promised_dock_date - actual_dock_date) per PO line. Per-(supplier, item_class): velocity(defect_rate, 30d), count(short_ship, 30d). Per-(carrier, lane): velocity(eta_revision, 24h), distribution(eta_error_sec, 30d), count(dwell_breach_at_geofence, 24h), p95(transit_time, 30d). Per-(shipment_id): age_seconds(last_telematics_ping), current_eta - promised_eta, count(geofence_dwell, current). Per-(po_id, asn_id): age_seconds(expected_dock_date - now), expected_qty - received_qty (short_ship signal). HLL / n_unique on (sku, store) pairs covered per period for cardinality bounding; top-K CMS on 'top-K SKUs by stock-out-velocity' / 'top-K stores by stock-out-velocity' / 'top-K suppliers by late-arrival rate' for analyst dashboards. The (sku, channel) attach-rate pair-aggregation overlaps directly with item 12's basket-affinity feature shape but the consumer here is the fulfillment-node-selection logic, not the pricing scorer.
domain_fit.entity_grain: Primary keys span sku / gtin / variant_id, (sku, store_id), (sku, dc_id), (sku, fc_id), (sku, zone_id), (sku, h3_cell), (sku, channel), (sku, customer_segment), (anchor_sku, candidate_sku, channel) pair, supplier_id, (supplier_id, sku) and (supplier_id, item_class) pairs, (carrier_id, lane_id), shipment_id, po_id, asn_id, fmi_device_id (Fastenal vending) / keepstock_device_id (Grainger), and tenant-scoped versions for multi-tenant OMS / control-tower vendors (Manhattan / Blue Yonder / project44 / FourKites SaaS).
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: Sliding windows dominate: 5m / 15m for stock-out velocity, ATP refresh, and reservation pressure (the BOPIS / ship-from-store hot path); 1h / 24h for short-cycle replenishment alerts; 7d / 30d / 90d for sell-through, days-of-cover, and supplier lead-time baselines. Tumbling windows on hourly / daily ticks for replenishment planner output (Walmart's pipeline ticks micro-batched). Hopping windows for the dynamic-reorder-point recalc. Approximate aggregates are widely acceptable: T-Digest for supplier lead-time and carrier ETA-error percentiles, CMS for top-K stock-out SKUs / top-K late-supplier views, HLL for n_unique(customer) per SKU per day. Exact aggregates are required for on_hand, allocated, soft_reserved, and ATP — overselling has direct customer-experience and regulatory (CCPA-adjacent disclosure) consequences. The on_hand counter is, in practice, the source of truth that drives oversell prevention; many published architectures back-stop beava-equivalent in-memory counters with an event-sourced ledger (Walmart's debit/credit, Confluent's event-sourcing patterns) so the live counter and the warehouse-of-record reconcile.
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: Strict no-double-count on on_hand / allocated / soft_reserved / ATP — overselling is the hard failure mode. At-least-once with idempotent counters keyed on event_id is acceptable for sell-through velocity, stock-out velocity, supplier-lead-time distributions, ETA-deviation features, and attach-rate counters. Walmart's published replenishment pipeline explicitly relies on an event-sourced debit/credit model exactly to make idempotency tractable; the standard pattern is to key beava counters on (event_id, op_type) and let WAL replay coalesce duplicates.

technical_fit.latency_budget: Three tiers. (a) Inline ATP / sourcing / promise-date / cart-add — strict tens to a couple hundred milliseconds end-to-end. ATP responses on a PDP add-to-cart or checkout reservation sit inside a 100-300 ms total budget of which the feature read should consume <20 ms; Redis-based ATP reference implementations (the Redis 'Available-to-Promise' tutorial) and Manhattan / Blue Yonder real-time order-streaming explicitly target sub-100 ms. (b) Auto-replenish / sourcing-decision tick — seconds to a few minutes (Walmart's 100M-SKU replenishment cycle is published as <3 hours, with intra-day micro-cycles at minute scale). (c) Control-tower ETA / dwell features — seconds for the alerting path. Beava's published sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get outperforms incumbent online-feature SLAs (Tecton sub-10ms p99, Hopsworks 7.5ms p99) and comfortably fits the inline ATP budget.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Sub-second to single-digit seconds for ATP / reservation / stock-out velocity on the omnichannel hot path (BOPIS, ship-from-store, ecom cart-add). Walmart's replenishment is intra-hour; Instacart's item-availability inference is described as 'real-time signals on the last observation' with sub-minute end-to-end latency. Supplier-lead-time and attach-rate features are minutes-to-hours fresh — bound by upstream ERP / EDI cadence (ASN, 856, 945) which is itself batch in many supplier ecosystems. Beava's push-on-event ingestion is materially fresher than the Kafka -> Flink -> Redis pipeline that Walmart, Instacart, project44, and FourKites publicly describe; the bottleneck for end-to-end freshness in supply chain is more often the upstream EDI / WMS event-bus than the in-memory aggregator. [uncertain]
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Highly buyer-dependent. (a) Tier-1 omnichannel retailer (Walmart, Amazon retail, Target): inventory event ingest at the hundreds-of-millions of events per day level, dominated by sale, receipt, allocation, reservation_open/release, and stock_count events. Walmart publishes ~500M inventory events/day plus 4B-message replenishment cycles, ~85 GB/min sustained on Kafka. Beava's ~684k EPS / core suffices for ~50B events/day per node sustained, which covers a regional Walmart-class deployment but not the full global aggregate without sharding. (b) Mid-market omnichannel retailer (Tesco, Costco, Best Buy, Carrefour): low millions to tens of millions of inventory-touch events/day, easily fits one node. (c) Grocery / quick-commerce platform (Instacart, DoorDash, Getir, Gorillas): tens of millions of item-availability inferences/day across ~100M items (Instacart published). (d) 3PL / control-tower (project44, FourKites, Shippeo, Transporeon): telematics pings + geofence dwells aggregated across thousands of customers — published as 1400+ telematics integrations at project44; gross volume in the low millions of EPS aggregate, easily per-region-shardable. (e) Industrial distributor with managed-inventory (Grainger KeepStock 65k+ devices; Fastenal FMI 44.9% of revenue from vending) — modest EPS but very fan-out heavy on (sku, device_id) state.
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Mixed by sub-path. Inline ATP / sourcing / promise-date is read-heavy 10:1 to 50:1 (every PDP view, search, cart-add reads ATP + per-node availability features; only checkouts write). Auto-replenishment and supplier-lead-time recalc is more write-heavy on the ingest side and read-heavy on the planner output side. Stock-count / RFID streams are write-heavy. Overall closer to balanced than the pricing or fraud verticals.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Dominated by (sku, store_id) and (sku, dc_id) composite-key cardinality. Tier-1 omnichannel: ~10-100M SKUs × 1000-5000 stores × ~30 active counter slots (sell_through_1h/24h/7d/30d, velocity, days_of_cover, on_hand, allocated, soft_reserved, ATP, stock_out_velocity, …) × ~32 B is unbounded without aggressive TTL — Walmart's published 100M SKUs × 4700+ stores implies ~470B (sku, store) pairs in principle but realistically <5% are active in any week (most SKUs sell at <100 stores), so the active hot state is ~10-50B pairs × ~30 counters × 32 B ≈ 10-50 TB — exceeds a single beava node by 2-3 orders of magnitude. Mid-market (~1-5M SKUs × 100-500 stores): ~50-500M active pairs × 30 × 32 B ≈ 50-500 GB, fits a single 256-512 GB node. 3PL visibility: 100k-1M active shipments × 20 counters × 32 B ≈ trivial; supplier graph ~10k-100k suppliers × 100-1000 item-classes ≈ negligible. Walmart-class buyers force sharding; mid-market omnichannel and 3PL control-tower fit one node. [uncertain]
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Slowly growing on SKU and supplier (catalog growth is bounded). Explosive on (sku, store_id), (sku, dc_id), (sku, zone_id), (sku, channel) composite keys (long tail of inactive pairs) — same shape as item 12 (pricing) but the active-pair density is even higher because operations cares about every node that ever stocked a SKU, while pricing concentrates on sellers/competitors. Bounded on (carrier_id, lane_id) (lanes are a finite graph), bounded on shipment_id during shipment lifetime (TTL on POD), bounded on po_id / asn_id (TTL on close). Top-K trending stockouts and top-K late suppliers are natural CMS / Top-K cases.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Short-fresh for ATP / reservation / stock-out velocity (1m / 5m / 15m sliding). Medium for sell-through, days-of-cover, attach-rate (7d / 30d / 90d). Long for supplier lead-time / on-time-rate baselines (180d-2y, but those baselines typically live in the warehouse and are refreshed into beava as scalar per-supplier baselines, same pattern as item 12). Per-shipment state evicts on POD + 1d; per-po_id state evicts on closeout + 30d (for receiving-discrepancy adjudication). Per-(sku, store) state evicts after 90d of zero activity. Per-RFID epc records are typically very short-lived (per-zone-read, per-scan).
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 20-80 features per fulfillment decision. ATP / promise-date at order-line level: 10-30 features per node × N candidate nodes (typically 5-10 nodes considered) = 50-200 batch reads per order line. Replenishment planner tick: 30-80 features per (SKU, DC). Stock-out prediction: 20-50 features per (SKU, store). Supplier-delay prediction: 20-40 features per (supplier, sku, po_line). All favour beava's batch_get path.
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Crash-safe is the baseline (a node losing its rolling 24h sell-through and on-hand counters for a recovery period is hours of degraded fulfillment accuracy, overselling, and missed reorders — millions in revenue impact on a Tier-1 retailer). Regulator-grade durability is required for the source-of-truth inventory ledger (warehoused, not beava — typically the WMS / OMS database, GS1 EPCIS event repository, SOX-relevant inventory valuations); the live counter tier is the appropriate beava scope. Walmart's published architecture explicitly separates the in-stream debit/credit ledger from the WMS-of-record. Beava's WAL + snapshot story covers the live-counter durability tier; the regulator-grade tier (SOX inventory valuation, GS1 EPCIS / DSCSA pharma serialization, FDA / EU FMD pharma traceability) stays in the warehouse / WMS.
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Strong fit for regional / per-DC / per-warehouse single-binary deployments next to a WMS or OMS shard. A per-region OMS-beava (US-East, EU, APAC), a per-DC WMS-beava, a per-region 3PL control-tower-beava, a per-tenant industrial-distributor beava (Grainger KeepStock, Fastenal FMI). Hard ceilings: beava v0 has no in-process sharding (global Walmart / Amazon / global Booking / global Manhattan SaaS aggregate exceeds a single box), no native multi-tenancy (Manhattan SaaS, Blue Yonder cloud, project44 / FourKites SaaS host many tenants), refuse-on-network-FS forces local-disk WAL planning (problematic for some cloud-WMS deployments that assume EFS-style storage), no built-in TLS/auth disqualifies any internet-exposed deployment (every OMS / WMS vendor needs SOC 2 / SOC 1 / sometimes ISO 27001 / PCI for checkout-adjacent paths), no multi-region active-active in v0.

commercial_fit.who_buys: Operations / fulfillment / supply-chain-engineering teams (distinct from pricing / RM which is item 12). Specifically: (a) omnichannel and big-box retailers (Walmart, Amazon retail, Target, Costco, Tesco, Sainsbury's, Carrefour, Ahold Delhaize, Kroger, Best Buy, Home Depot, Lowe's, Macy's, Nordstrom, Marks & Spencer, Zara/Inditex, H&M, Uniqlo, IKEA, MediaMarkt, Currys, Wayfair); (b) quick-commerce / grocery e-com (Instacart, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Getir, Gorillas, Picnic, Ocado); (c) 3PL / 4PL operators and digital-freight (DHL Supply Chain, XPO, GXO, Ryder, NFI, RXO, CH Robinson, Coyote, Flexport, ArcBest, Werner); (d) real-time transportation visibility platforms (project44, FourKites, Shippeo, Transporeon, Descartes, Vizion, Tive, Roambee); (e) OMS / WMS / DOM vendors (Manhattan Associates, Blue Yonder, Oracle Fusion SCM, IBM Sterling Order Management, SAP EWM, Infios, Aptean Logility, Tecsys, Körber, Softeon, Fluent Commerce, Kibo, KBRW, OneStock, Deck Commerce, Magestore, NetSuite, Brightpearl); (f) industrial distribution and managed-inventory (Grainger KeepStock, Fastenal FMI, Würth, MSC Industrial, HD Supply, Bunzl); (g) fashion / specialty retailers with ship-from-store strategies (Inditex, H&M, Boohoo, ASOS, Zalando, JD Sports); (h) DTC brands using Shopify / commercetools / Adobe Commerce who outgrew built-in inventory and want a real-time aggregator. The buyer persona is VP Supply Chain Engineering / Director of Fulfillment Tech / Distinguished Engineer on the OMS or WMS team — explicitly not the merchandising / pricing / RM persona who buys item 12.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: Multiple adjacent markets converge here. Order Management Software market: USD ~3-5B in 2024-2025, projected USD 5.7-13B by 2032-2035 across multiple market-research sources (Forrester forecasts the global OMS market reaching ~USD 1.9B by 2026 in the narrow definition; SnS Insider / Markets and Markets / Metastat Insight project 5-7B in 2024 broader scope; Emergen Research forecasts USD 13B by 2035 in the multichannel-OMS bucket). Distributed Order Management (DOM) subsegment: USD 1.5B (2026) -> USD 3.8B (2033) at 10.8% CAGR per OpenPR / Nucleus Research. Warehouse Management System (WMS) market: USD 2.8-4.4B (2026) -> USD 10.6B (2034) per Fortune Business Insights / Grand View Research / Market Growth Reports. Real-time transportation visibility platform market: project44 + FourKites + Shippeo + Transporeon + Descartes have a combined ARR in the high hundreds of millions to low billions of dollars; the segment is one of the fastest growing in logistics tech. Vendor scale signals: Manhattan Associates passed USD 1B in annual revenue in 2024 (joining SAP, Blue Yonder, Oracle in the 'billion-dollar SCM club'); Blue Yonder is private-equity owned (Panasonic / Blackstone history) with ~USD 1B+ ARR; Oracle Fusion SCM and SAP EWM/IBP are multi-billion-dollar lines inside their parents; Manhattan Active OMS is the published Gartner Magic Quadrant leader for distributed order management. Adjacent: Confluent's published retail customer base (Walmart, Instacart, Ulta, Lowe's, Target via various case studies) is a direct funnel for real-time-inventory feature backends. [uncertain]
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: 1) Omnichannel maturity: 99% of retailers committing to same-day delivery by 2025 (Supply Chain Dive); BOPIS / ship-from-store / curbside pickup are now table stakes and they all require sub-second cross-channel inventory accuracy. 2) Post-COVID supply-chain disruption: persistent supplier-lead-time variance through 2023-2026 has driven retailer investment in dynamic lead-time prediction (AWS, GAINSystems, SAP IBP all rolled out ML-based lead-time products 2023-2026). 3) The 2026 OMS/WMS convergence wave (Nucleus Research 2026 OMS Value Matrix, Gartner Distributed Order Management Magic Quadrant, Logistics Viewpoints 'Digital Backbone of the Warehouse 2026' coverage) — every Tier-1 omnichannel retailer is in the middle of replacing legacy OMS / WMS with cloud-native event-driven platforms. 4) RFID / item-level tracking adoption: Walmart's RFID mandate expansion (2022-2026), Target's RFID rollout, Inditex's chip-on-tag rollout — all generate the high-cardinality (sku, store_id, zone_id, epc) event streams that drive in-memory aggregation. 5) 3PL / control-tower platform consolidation: project44's Movement platform, FourKites' AI control tower (Kai Waehner 2025 case study), and the Descartes / Transporeon competitive race force real-time SLA improvements across the visibility-platform market. 6) Returns-loss pressure and the Optoro / Blue Yonder 2025 acquisition expanded WMS-embedded returns to the OMS surface — returns velocity is the next big counter. 7) Industrial-distribution vending: Fastenal FMI is now 44.9% of revenue, Grainger KeepStock represents ~USD 1B in annual sales — both depend on (device_id, sku) telemetry feeds that beava is a natural fit for. 8) Demand-volatility / tariff / geopolitical pressure through 2024-2026 drives supplier-diversification and supplier-lead-time-tracking investment.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: SOX (US) requires auditable inventory valuation for public retailers, but this lives in the WMS / ERP-of-record, not beava live counters. GDPR / CCPA apply to any (customer_id, sku, store_id) attach-rate features that include personally identifiable customer keys — right-to-erasure must cascade through derived aggregates (the same blocker as item 12). PCI-DSS scope expands when inventory features sit adjacent to checkout. PCI scope is mitigated when beava holds only SKU and node counters, not card data. GS1 EPCIS / DSCSA (Drug Supply Chain Security Act, US, fully effective Nov 2023 with 2024-2025 stabilization period) and EU FMD require pharma serial-level traceability for prescription drug distribution — beava is well-suited to hold per-serial in-flight counters but not the regulator-grade serialized event repository, which is mandated to be persisted and queryable for ≥6 years. FSMA 204 / FDA Food Traceability Rule (compliance date Jan 2026, extended from earlier) requires lot-level traceability for designated foods on the FTL list — same architecture: beava can serve live per-lot velocity, but the audit ledger stays in the warehouse. EU Forced Labour Regulation and EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) drive supplier-traceability investment but do not directly constrain in-memory counters. EU Digital Product Passport (DPP, ESPR, phased 2025-2030) will eventually constrain SKU-level traceability events. SOC 2 Type II is table stakes for any enterprise OMS / WMS / 3PL procurement.
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: Fast — 3-7 days to a working per-(SKU, store) sell-through + days-of-cover + stock-out velocity demo on beava, since @bv.event + @bv.table primitives map directly to published feature definitions (sell-through, days-of-cover, ATP, reservation pressure). A realistic 30-80-feature production pilot at a mid-market omnichannel retailer or a single-region 3PL control tower is a 4-10 week effort once TLS, auth, multi-tenancy, and OMS / WMS event-bridge connectors (SAP IDoc, EDI 856/940/945, Manhattan event streams, Blue Yonder event streams, project44 / FourKites webhooks) are added. The natural one-page README example for this vertical is a 'real-time stock-out and reorder' demo with sale / receipt / stock_count events keyed on (sku, store_id), which complements the existing python/beava/demos/ecommerce demo on the buyer side.

competition.incumbents: Generic stream-processing stack dominated by Kafka + Flink / Kafka Streams / ksqlDB for the windowing layer and Redis / Aerospike / DynamoDB / Cassandra / Scylla for the low-latency ATP / counter store. Walmart's published architecture is Kafka + Spark Streaming + in-house micro-batch processors + an event-sourced debit/credit ledger across 18 brokers / 20+ topics / 500+ partitions. Instacart's item-availability stack is Kafka + Confluent + their own Griffin feature store. DoorDash's Iguazu is Kafka + Flink at ~100B events/day. Confluent Cloud is the published platform for Instacart, Walmart, Ulta, Lowe's, and many other Tier-1 retailers. The 'Redis for real-time inventory' pattern (with WATCH/MULTI for atomic reservations, Lua for ATP, Redis Streams for event sourcing) is documented in Redis's own tutorials and is the de-facto reference for mid-market omnichannel. Online feature-store generic competitors: Tecton (dynamic pricing is a flagship use case, less so inventory but architecturally similar), Hopsworks (RonDB, 250k+ ops/sec, called out for manufacturing / supply chain in some materials), Chalk, Feast (open-source), Fennel (Rust-native streaming feature store), Databricks Feature Store. Adjacent: Materialize / RisingWave / ksqlDB / Feldera for SQL-on-streams aggregation pipelines; ScyllaDB / Aerospike / DynamoDB as low-latency KV stores.
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: Direct domain-specific incumbents (would either embed beava as their counter backend or compete head-on at the decision layer): Distributed Order Management / OMS — Manhattan Active Omni / OMS, Blue Yonder OMS (formerly Yantriks / JDA), Oracle Retail Order Management / Oracle Fusion Order Management, IBM Sterling Order Management, SAP S/4HANA Order Management, Fluent Commerce, KBRW, Kibo, OneStock, Deck Commerce, HotWax Commerce, NetSuite OMS, Brightpearl, ChannelEngine, Linnworks, Cin7, Veeqo, Magestore. competition.beava_differentiator: 1) Single binary, no Kafka / Flink / Redis cluster — fits per-region / per-DC / per-warehouse sidecar topologies that mid-market OMS / WMS vendors (Fluent Commerce, KBRW, Kibo, OneStock, Deck Commerce, HotWax, NetSuite, Brightpearl, Magestore) and many per-DC in-house teams actually deploy. 2) 50+ aggregation primitives natively cover sell-through / days-of-cover / reservation-pressure / stock-out-velocity / supplier-lead-time / ETA-deviation / attach-rate features, no Lua / Flink-SQL / Spark Streaming needed. 3) Sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get fits the tens-of-ms inline ATP and DOM-sourcing-decision budget with material headroom; in published benchmarks beava is the same order of magnitude faster than Tecton's stated sub-10 ms p99 and Hopsworks' 7.5 ms p99 — both already faster than Walmart / Instacart's published Kafka + Redis pipelines. 4) Native composite-key (pair / triple) aggregations — (sku, store_id), (sku, dc_id), (sku, channel), (sku, zone_id), (supplier_id, sku), (carrier_id, lane_id), (anchor_sku, candidate_sku, channel) — which Redis requires hand-rolled hash-of-hash schemes for and which are exactly the keying shape OMS / WMS buyers want. 5) Apache-2.0, no open-core — attractive to mid-market OMS vendors (Fluent Commerce, KBRW, Kibo, OneStock, HotWax, Magestore, Deck Commerce, NetSuite, Brightpearl, Cin7, Veeqo) who want to embed it without paying Tecton, and to large in-house teams (Walmart, Target, Costco, Tesco, Carrefour, Inditex, Best Buy) who do not want vendor lock-in on a margin-critical control plane. 6) Distance primitive cleanly expresses 'promised_eta - current_eta', 'promised_lead_time - actual_lead_time', 'days_of_cover - safety_stock_days' — load-bearing supply-chain features. 7) Push-on-event ingestion matches how the supply-chain stack already emits events: SAP IDoc, EDI 856/940/945, GS1 EPCIS, RFID middleware, OMS event topics, WMS event topics, project44 / FourKites webhooks — no broker hop, no Kafka cluster needed for small / mid deployments. 8) Sliding windows over 7d / 30d / 90d align directly with the published industry feature definitions (sell-through, days-of-cover, on-time-rate, lead-time percentile). 9) The reservation / release / allocation lifecycle expresses cleanly as @bv.event with idempotent counters, the canonical 'ATP without Redis WATCH/MULTI' pattern.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: 1) No TLS, no auth in v0 on :8080 / :8081 / :8090 — disqualifying for SOC 2 / SOC 1 / PCI-adjacent OMS or WMS deployments and for any internet-exposed control tower (project44, FourKites SaaS). Same blocker as items 1a / 9 / 10 / 12 — the most important single gap. 2) No in-process sharding — global Walmart / Amazon retail / global Manhattan SaaS / global Blue Yonder SaaS aggregate exceeds a single box; the single-tenant ceiling is roughly ~684k EPS and ~100-150 GB hot state, so multi-region Tier-1 retailers and multi-tenant WMS SaaS need sharding. 3) Refuse-on-network-FS plus in-memory-only forces local-disk WAL planning and bounds cold-start replay time — must be benchmarked for tens of GB of (sku, store) hot state. 4) No triggers / 'fire callback when (sku, store).days_of_cover < 3 then call /reorder' or 'when (sku, store).stock_out_velocity > N then disable for online sale and mark substitute' — fulfillment is fundamentally event-driven (auto-reorder, auto-substitute, auto-rebalance, auto-mark-unavailable), and polling 30-80 features per tick on every (sku, store) pair is wasteful at the Tier-1 cardinality. 5) No native multi-tenancy primitives — Manhattan SaaS, Blue Yonder SaaS, project44 SaaS, FourKites SaaS, Fluent Commerce, KBRW, OneStock, Deck Commerce, Magestore SaaS, NetSuite OMS all host many tenants on shared infra; per-tenant namespaces, quotas, per-tenant rate-limit accounting are required. 6) No secondary indexes / no 'list all (sku, store) with stock_out_velocity > N' or 'top-K late suppliers in last 30d' analyst surface — kills the operations-dashboard / planner-UI surface that every OMS / WMS / control-tower ships. 7) No native EDI / SAP IDoc / GS1 EPCIS / RFID-middleware / WMS-event ingest connectors — every existing supply-chain stack assumes a broker or an integration platform (Boomi, MuleSoft, IBM Sterling B2B Integrator, SAP CPI). 8) No native point-in-time backfill / time-travel — needed for lead-time-prediction model training to avoid future leakage. 9) No oversell-prevention primitive — atomic-decrement-with-watch (Redis WATCH/MULTI semantics) is the canonical pattern; beava's atomic counters help but the 'reject if negative' / 'reserve up to N' compare-and-set semantics are not first-class. 10) No native pharma (DSCSA / FMD) or food (FSMA 204) serialized-traceability event-repository — beava can serve live counters but not the regulator-grade ledger. 11) No multi-region active-active for global retailers. 12) Documented Kafka / Confluent / Flink / EDI-translator ingest patterns are critical to ship — every Tier-1 retailer's source-of-events stack assumes one of these.

competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Both. Fulfillment is uniquely a hybrid of deterministic rules (sourcing rules: 'ship from nearest node with on_hand > order_qty', 'don't ship hazmat from store X', 'split shipments only if cost_diff < threshold', 'protect safety stock for in-store traffic') and ML (lead-time prediction, stock-out prediction, item-availability scoring, dynamic-reorder-point ML). Both consume the same per-(sku, store) sell-through / days-of-cover / reservation-pressure features from beava via batch_get.

adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: Mostly passive load with limited adversarial sub-paths. The dominant load is passive: sale, receipt, reservation, stock_count, telematics. Adversarial sub-paths exist but are narrower than fraud / anti-abuse domains: (1) Amazon-3P and marketplace sellers gaming reorder-velocity or attach-rate features to manipulate Buy Box / placement (mostly an item 12 problem). (2) Returns abuse and 'wardrobing' that distorts net-sell-through. (3) Bot-driven inventory-scraping that biases reservation-velocity counters. (4) Inside-job inventory shrink that biases on_hand counters away from reality (the RFID / cycle-count correction signal helps). (5) Supplier gaming of on-time-rate metrics around contract SLAs. Feature drift is generally seasonal and supply-shock-driven (post-COVID, tariff, weather, port disruption) rather than fraudster-driven — meaning periodic retraining is sufficient and the feature-add cadence is closer to dynamic pricing (item 12) than to fraud (item 1a).

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: 1) The replenishment optimizer / order-orchestration engine itself — that is the proprietary IP of Blue Yonder, Manhattan, Oracle, RELEX, ToolsGroup, o9, Aptean Logility, SAP IBP, IBM Sterling. Beava is the feature backend, not the planner or the OMS. 2) The inventory ledger of record / source of truth — Walmart's debit/credit pattern, SAP S/4HANA, Oracle ERP, Manhattan WMS database, Microsoft Dynamics ERP all own that role with regulator-grade durability and SOX-relevant audit trails; beava is the in-memory live aggregator that sits in front of it. 3) Regulator-grade serialized traceability ledgers — DSCSA / FMD pharma (≥6 years retention, regulator-queryable), FSMA 204 food traceability, EU FMD, EU DPP / ESPR product passport, GS1 EPCIS event repository — all warehouse-of-record concerns. Beava can serve live in-flight serial-level counters; the audit ledger sits in dedicated systems (TraceLink, IBM Food Trust, rfXcel, Antares Vision). 4) Long-horizon forecasting (LSTM, Prophet, DeepAR, temporal-fusion transformer, hierarchical reconciliation) — beava provides the historical aggregates the forecaster consumes; the forecaster lives elsewhere (RELEX, ToolsGroup, AWS Supply Chain). 5) Yard management, dock scheduling, labor management, slotting optimization — those are WMS / WES (warehouse-execution-system) concerns. Beava can hold the live dwell / utilization counters but is not the planner. 6) Returns-disposition optimization (Optoro / Blue Yonder) — beava can hold returns velocity counters but not the disposition rules. 7) Multi-echelon inventory optimization (MEIO) — solver-class problem; beava is feature backend only. 8) Detailed shop-floor MES integration (Aveva, Rockwell, Siemens MOM) — out of scope. 9) Multi-region active-active in v0. 10) Direct EDI translation — beava expects events post-translation from a connector layer (IBM Sterling B2B Integrator, SPS Commerce, OpenText, Boomi, MuleSoft, Cleo); shipping a translator is out of scope. 11) The cold-chain temperature / humidity ledger for pharma / food (that is dedicated IoT-telemetry territory and is closer to item 13 than item 27).
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship to be production-grade for supply chain / inventory, in priority order: 1) TLS termination and mutual TLS on :8080 / :8081 / :8090 plus an auth model (token, mTLS, or both) on the push and admin surfaces — without this, no SOC 2 / SOC 1 / PCI-adjacent OMS / WMS / 3PL / control-tower can deploy externally. This is the same blocker that limits items 1a / 9 / 10 / 12 — the single most important gap. 2) Triggers / 'fire callback when (sku, store).days_of_cover < 3 then call /reorder' or 'when (sku, store).stock_out_velocity > N then disable_for_online_sale and propose substitute' or 'when (supplier_id).late_arrival_rate_30d > 0.05 then de-prioritize in sourcing' — fulfillment is fundamentally event-driven and polling 20-80 features per (sku, store) pair on every tick is wasteful at Walmart-scale cardinality. 3) Compare-and-set / atomic-decrement-with-watch / 'reserve-up-to-N' primitives — the canonical Redis WATCH/MULTI ATP semantic — to prevent oversell at the ATP / reservation_open layer. Beava's atomic counters are necessary but not sufficient. 4) First-class composite-key (pair / triple) aggregations with ergonomic @bv.table syntax — (sku, store_id), (sku, dc_id), (sku, zone_id), (sku, channel), (supplier_id, sku), (supplier_id, item_class), (carrier_id, lane_id), (anchor_sku, candidate_sku, channel), (sku, h3_cell). 5) HLL / Bloom / CMS / Top-K as first-class aggregations and document the natural supply-chain analyst queries ('top-K SKUs by stock-out velocity in last 24h', 'top-K stores by reservation-release rate', 'top-K late suppliers by lead-time-delta'). 6) In-process or sidecar sharding by key prefix (sku, store_id) for Tier-1 retailer scale (Walmart / Amazon retail / global Inditex). 7) Per-key TTL / sliding-window eviction aligned with supply-chain windows (5m / 15m / 1h / 24h / 7d / 30d / 90d) so (sku, store) cardinality stays bounded by activity. 8) Multi-tenancy: per-tenant namespaces, quotas, per-tenant rate-limit accounting for SaaS OMS / WMS / control-tower vendors (Manhattan SaaS, Blue Yonder SaaS, Fluent Commerce, KBRW, Kibo, OneStock, project44, FourKites, NetSuite, Brightpearl, Magestore SaaS). 9) Time-travel / point-in-time backfill for lead-time-prediction / stock-out-prediction model training — required to avoid future leakage. 10) Documented Kafka / Confluent / Kinesis / Flink / EDI-translator / SAP-event-mesh / Manhattan-Active-event-bus / Blue-Yonder-event-bus / project44 / FourKites ingest patterns — every existing supply-chain buyer's source-of-events stack assumes a broker or an integration platform. 11) Secondary indexes and a streaming admin / debug surface so operations / planners can run 'list (sku, store) with days_of_cover < 3' without materializing the whole keyspace — every OMS / WMS dashboard needs this. 12) PII-handling story: any (customer_id, sku) attach-rate feature must support hashing at rest, configurable per-namespace retention, right-to-erasure cascade through derived aggregates (GDPR / CCPA). 13) Cold-start strategy: WAL replay on tens of GB of (sku, store) state must be benchmarked and bounded; OMS / WMS recovery SLOs are typically minutes, not hours. 14) Reference architecture for the inventory-of-record reconciliation pattern (live beava counters + event-sourced ledger + SOX-relevant ERP/WMS-of-record). 15) Documented bridges to GS1 EPCIS, RFID middleware (Impinj, Zebra), and EDI translators (Cleo, Boomi, MuleSoft, IBM B2BI). 16) Optional: pharma DSCSA / food FSMA 204 / EU DPP scaffolding for serial-level live counters with documented hand-off to the regulator-grade serialized-event-repository. 17) Multi-region active-active replication once a buyer exceeds single-region.
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes — strongly. Supply chain / inventory is genuinely event-driven and needs first-class trigger primitives: 'when (sku, store).days_of_cover < target then call /reorder API', 'when (sku, store).stock_out_velocity_5m > N then disable online sale and propose substitute', 'when (sku, dc).on_hand < safety_stock then call /transfer_request', 'when (supplier_id).on_time_rate_30d < 0.9 then call /alert and tag PO for review', 'when (carrier_id, lane_id).eta_revision_rate_24h > N then re-route', 'when (shipment_id).dwell_at_geofence > N minutes then call /late_shipment_alert', 'when (sku, store).reservation_pressure_15m crosses N then increase node-allocation priority'. Polling 20-80 features per (sku, store, supplier, lane, shipment) on every tick is workable on the read path but is wasteful and high-latency on the asynchronous auto-reorder / auto-substitute / auto-rebalance / dispatcher-alert path — together with TLS + auth this is one of the two most-cited engineering gaps for the domain.
